summary: Validated (validate --run <run> --submission update25.json → valid=true). New A1 direction on leadership stability: a configuration-validation gap with a documented-purpose mismatch. The field's own doc says the lease controls how long the leader may go 'without being able to contact a quorum of nodes', and the check measures contact as the elapsed time since each follower's last response versus the lease, stepping down when fewer than a quorum are contacted (raft.go:1036-1080). The leader's ability to speak to its followers, however, is bounded by its own timers: a heartbeat every random interval up to one tenth of the heartbeat timeout (replication.go:398-405) plus a commit-timeout re-replication (replication.go:163-172). So the relation that makes the monitor meaningful is a lower bound on the lease relative to that cadence — and validation enforces only a five-millisecond floor and an upper bound of the full heartbeat timeout, alongside requiring the election timeout to be at least the heartbeat timeout (config.go:366-374). A configuration such as a one-second heartbeat timeout with a five-millisecond lease is therefore accepted, and in it the check reports a contact failure and steps down while responses are arriving normally; re-election reproduces the configuration, so the outcome is repeated leadership loss with no sustained progress — a deterministic mechanism gated only by a configuration the library accepts, not a race. Recorded as one Fact, an active question with an executed-witness discriminator, and an 'explained' interpretation, graded honestly: the default lease is half the heartbeat timeout and far above the cadence, so this is a validation gap rather than a defect of the default, but the impact when it occurs is that a cluster cannot keep a leader. Counterevidence kept explicit — contact is refreshed by any response including a rejection (so the effective cadence is at least the commit-timeout interval), the situation is diagnosable from the check's log line and transition metric, and the mis-firing threshold is deployment-dependent (latency, commit timeout) and was not measured.
